wiki-iran.standing: Daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on Iran — a country of roughly 90 million people whose oil exports, nuclear programme and control of one shore of the Strait of Hormuz make it a recurring subject of global attention.
wiki-iran.recent: Readership has fallen by roughly a quarter from its 19 July peak as the Hormuz standoff shifted from confrontation to negotiation. Iran keeps the strait closed pending six conditions and a reparations clause, with 8 to 15 ships crossing daily; Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the exchanges with Washington are messages, not talks.

brent.standing: The price of a barrel of North Sea crude, and the benchmark most of the world's oil is priced against. It moves on supply — a strike, a sanction, a strait — and fuel, freight and fertiliser move after it.
brent.recent: Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz closed, with 8 to 15 ships crossing daily and reopening still conditional on six demands; Trump halted his attack on Iran on 2 August and then claimed the US fully controls the strait. Prices sit well below the May 18 high of 116.7, but above the July 2 low, with strikes on Jazan and Nizhnekamsk refineries keeping a war premium in diesel.

wti.standing: The price of a barrel of US light sweet crude, the American oil benchmark and the settlement price for the world's most heavily traded oil futures contract. Refiners, airlines and truckers price their fuel against it.
wti.recent: The war premium is unwinding faster than the war. Crude has fallen through the 56-day window even as Ukrainian drones hit two Russian refineries and killed 13 at Nizhnekamsk, because those strikes destroy refining capacity rather than crude supply; futures eased further on Trump's 'good talks' comment on Iran and on Hormuz reopening hopes.

natgas-hh.standing: The US benchmark price for natural gas, set at a Louisiana pipeline hub and quoted per million British thermal units. It prices the fuel that heats American homes, runs much of the power grid, and feeds LNG cargoes sold abroad.
natgas-hh.recent: Gas has drifted down through the summer, from $3.34 in late May to $2.81, with the low of $2.58 set on 29 July. Nothing in the current news explains the slide; what the period does show is demand being built rather than priced — Amazon funding a 35-turbine Texas plant beside a data centre, and SpaceX building its own gas plants in Grimes County rather than wait on the grid.

wheat.standing: The world price of a tonne of wheat, the cereal that feeds more people directly than any other. It moves on harvests, export policy and the cost of fertiliser and fuel, and bread prices follow it into importing countries within months.
wheat.recent: Wheat has climbed off its September 2025 low of $155.1 to $199.6, peaking at $220.9 in May 2026, and the pass-through is visible downstream: the FAO's food price index hit 131.1, US diesel at $5.36 a gallon is lifting freight into every cereal chain, and a 20kg flour bag in Karachi now costs Rs3,000.

rice.standing: The world benchmark price for a tonne of milled rice, the staple calorie for more than half the planet. It moves on monsoon rainfall, export bans and stockpiling, and it passes almost directly into household food bills across Asia and West Africa.
rice.recent: Rice has fallen 29% over the series and sits near the October 2025 low of $330.6, well below its August 2024 high — a divergence from cereals generally, with the Food and Agriculture Organization's price index at 131.1 as heatwaves and wars push up crop costs. A second monsoon spell arriving on saturated ground in Pakistan puts a major exporter's crop at risk.

copper.standing: The price of a tonne of refined copper, the metal that carries electricity in every grid, motor, transformer and building. Demand for it tracks electrification and construction directly, which is why it is read as a gauge of industrial expansion.
copper.recent: Copper sits at its series high of $13,550/mt in June 2026, roughly half again above the $8,910 low of December 2024. The input does not name the supply or demand event behind the rise.

us-10y.standing: The yield on ten-year US government debt, the benchmark price of borrowing dollars for a decade. Mortgages, corporate loans and asset prices worldwide are priced off it, so a move here reprices almost everything else.
us-10y.recent: The Fed held rates at 350-375 basis points on 29 July, citing elevated, fuel-led inflation, and the yield peaked at 4.75% two days later. It has since eased to 4.65% as a further hike fell into doubt — the same repricing that dragged the dollar to its weakest since May on 7 August.

sp500.standing: A capitalisation-weighted index of 500 large American companies, and the standard benchmark for US equities. Trillions in pension and index-fund money track it, so its level is also the mark on ordinary retirement accounts.
sp500.recent: The climb ran through late July on the AI trade: Microsoft topped quarterly cloud growth estimates, easing spending concerns, while Alphabet's stock fell 7% on the same capex it used to cheer. The Fed then held interest rates steady citing 'elevated' inflation, and stocks gained on Hormuz reopening hopes as oil eased into the Aug 7 high.

nasdaq100.standing: A stock index tracking the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq exchange, weighted by market value. It is dominated by American technology firms, which makes it the closest thing markets have to a price on the software and semiconductor trade.
nasdaq100.recent: The index sits near the top of its 61-day range after a run of AI-infrastructure commitments: Nvidia said it will partner with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR on financing vehicles totalling more than $500 billion, and Amazon is funding a Texas gas plant to power AI data centres. Component costs are rising too — TrendForce puts DRAM at $145, up from $39.

us-gas-retail.standing: The average price American drivers pay at the pump, tracked weekly by the Energy Information Administration. It follows crude oil with a lag of a few weeks, and passes through to freight costs, household budgets and the politics of an election year.
us-gas-retail.recent: Ukraine's drone campaign has moved from the border to Russia's refining interior — Ryazan on 29 July, two refineries including Yaroslavl on 6 August, and Nizhnekamsk on 10 August, 1,600 km from the Ukrainian border and 13 dead. Houthi strikes also shut Aramco's 400,000-bpd Jazan refinery on 28 July.

natgas-ttf.standing: The European benchmark price for wholesale natural gas, set at a Dutch virtual trading hub. It is what the continent's power stations, heating and heavy industry pay for gas, and it moves on pipeline and LNG supply.
natgas-ttf.recent: Supply infrastructure has been the pressure point. A drone strike on floating storage at Egypt's Damietta LNG terminal on 29 July set fire to one tanker and then a second, and the Nord Stream sabotage remains unresolved, with Russia pressing Germany to identify those behind the blasts.

vix.standing: A measure of how much movement traders expect in the S&P 500 over the coming month, priced from index options. It falls when markets are calm and spikes when they are frightened, which is why it is read as an equity fear gauge.
vix.recent: Volatility has drained out of risk assets since the June peak. The same calm shows up in bitcoin, where volatility nearly vanished as ETFs took in $754 million, and traders described the sell-off from $65,000 as thin volume rather than panic selling. Equities boomed into the end of July.

fx-pkr.standing: The exchange rate of Pakistan's rupee against the US dollar. Pakistan imports most of its fuel, wheat and industrial inputs, so the rate sets the domestic price of energy and food and the cost of servicing external debt.
fx-pkr.recent: The rupee has been near-flat over the month, trading in a narrow band between 276.5 and 279.2. The pressures around it are fiscal and political rather than monetary: the finance ministry warned inflation would reach 9-10% on external war transmission, a 20kg flour bag now costs Rs3,000 after a delayed wheat import tender, and Jamaat-e-Islami counted 510 protests in a day against the petroleum levy.

fx-ngn.standing: The exchange rate of Nigeria's currency against the US dollar. Nigeria imports most of its refined fuel, wheat and medicine, so the naira's level sets domestic prices, and oil earnings in dollars are the main thing propping it up.
fx-ngn.recent: The naira has been broadly flat, easing from 1,386 on Jul 14 to 1,358 on Jul 31 before settling near current levels — a move of roughly one percent across the month, well inside ordinary trading noise. The political news out of Nigeria in this window, from the Osun election dispute to Tinubu's order that the EFCC vacate the Osun account freeze, has not shifted it.

fx-egp.standing: The exchange rate between Egypt's currency and the US dollar, quoted as pounds per dollar. Egypt imports most of its wheat, fuel and medicine, so the rate sets the domestic price of nearly everything on a shelf.
fx-egp.recent: The pound has firmed over the past month, from 51.37 to the dollar on Jul 25 to 49.56 on Aug 8, its strongest level in the window, before easing back to 49.97. Nothing in the available reporting accounts for the turn.

fx-try.standing: The Turkish lira against the US dollar, the price at which Turkey's currency trades. It sets the cost of everything Turkey imports — energy, machinery, grain — and it is the number Turkish households watch to judge whether their savings are holding value.
fx-try.recent: The lira slid to 47.73 to the dollar, its weakest of the past month, against a run of security news rather than economic news: Turkey's parliament passed a law dissolving and disarming the PKK, Ankara signed a joint defence pact in Mecca with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, and drones struck the Turkish-operated cargo ship Nadezhda near Novorossiysk.

fx-bdt.standing: The Bangladeshi taka's exchange rate against the US dollar, quoted as taka per dollar, so a rising number means a weaker taka. It prices the imported fuel, food and industrial inputs behind the country's garment export trade, and sets what remittances from abroad are worth at home.
fx-bdt.recent: The taka drifted about 0.06% weaker over the month, reaching 124 to the dollar on 7 August, its weakest of the period, against a low of 122.7 on 16 July. The window covers a diplomatic strain with Delhi, which denied involvement in ex-Bangladesh PM Hasina's planned speech, but nothing in it explains a move this small.

fx-idr.standing: Indonesia's currency, quoted as rupiah per US dollar, so a higher number means a weaker rupiah. Southeast Asia's largest economy runs on commodity exports, and the rate sets the price of imported fuel, food and dollar debt.
fx-idr.recent: The rupiah has firmed about 1.8% over the past month, from 18,140 on 13 July to 17,800 on 8 August. Nothing in the Indonesian news of the window explains the move: the period's stories were a Madura ferry fire, deepening losses at the Whoosh high-speed rail line, and a drought-driven salt harvest in Cirebon.

fx-lbp.standing: The exchange rate between Lebanon's pound and the US dollar. After the 2019 banking collapse wiped out most of its value, the rate was refixed far below the old peg, and it now sets the price of nearly everything in a country that imports most of what it consumes.
fx-lbp.recent: The pound has held almost flat for a month, moving less than a quarter of a percent while the south burned. Israeli strikes and demolitions continued through the ceasefire — Lebanese officials count 4,333 killed in the south since March — and a seventh round of direct talks in Rome produced no halt. None of it moved the rate.

fx-cny.standing: The exchange rate between China's currency and the US dollar, managed within a band the People's Bank of China sets each morning. It is the price at which the world's largest exporter converts its earnings, so it moves the cost of Chinese goods everywhere.
fx-cny.recent: The yuan drifted to the strong end of its 30-day range, gaining about half a percent since 13 July with the low on 11 August. Nothing in the period's China news explains the move directly: the largest disruptions were Typhoon Dolphin, which forced port closures and over a million evacuations before landfall, and weak China demand behind Mercedes' cut sales outlook.

fx-inr.standing: The rupee's exchange rate against the US dollar, the price at which India's currency trades. India imports most of its crude oil, so a weaker rupee raises the domestic cost of fuel, and it sets the return foreign investors take home.
fx-inr.recent: The rupee traded in a narrow band, ending near 95.4 to the dollar after a high of 96.65 on Jul 18 and a low of 95.05 on Aug 5. The one policy shock in view is a US Senate bill threatening 100% tariffs on India, which would hit the export earnings that supply the country's dollars. Nothing else in the window explains the drift.

fx-brl.standing: Brazil's currency, quoted as reais per US dollar, so a rising number means a weaker real. It is one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies, and it moves on commodity prices, domestic politics and the gap between Brazilian and US interest rates.
fx-brl.recent: The real held in a narrow band through a month of friction with Washington. Brazil requested WTO consultations over US tariffs on 28 July, and on 4 August the US revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador, saying it would restore it if Brasília accepted its own envoy pick. Lula was nominated for a fourth term on 2 August.

fx-mxn.standing: The Mexican peso against the US dollar, one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies and a round-the-clock proxy for sentiment on Mexico's economy and its relationship with Washington. Trade, remittances and manufacturing all price through it.
fx-mxn.recent: The peso firmed to 17.14 from a 17.54 peak on Jul 19, its strongest level in the window, through a month in which Mexico's news flow was security and public health rather than macro: the US posted a $25 million bounty on a CJNG leader, the Sinaloa Cartel split into warring factions, human screwworm cases passed 500, and Mexico and Peru restored diplomatic relations. None of that explains the move.

fx-eur.standing: The euro against the US dollar, the world's second-most traded currency pair and the price at which the eurozone's savings, trade and debt are converted into the global reserve currency. Its level sets what Europe pays for imported energy and commodities.
fx-eur.recent: The euro drifted down over the month, from 0.8792 on Jul 26 to a low of 0.8651 on Aug 8, with no single event in the record accounting for the move. The period's European news was structural rather than monetary: Spain imposing border checks on Italy, Berlin doubling its anti-drone force after an explosive-laden drone was found at Leipzig/Halle Airport, and IRIS2's cost climbing to €15.6 billion.

fx-jpy.standing: The exchange rate of Japan's currency against the US dollar, quoted as yen per dollar, so a higher number is a weaker yen. It sets the value of Japanese exporters' overseas earnings and funds the carry trade that borrows cheap yen to buy higher-yielding assets abroad.
fx-jpy.recent: Tokyo sold dollars for yen hours before the Bank of Japan held rates at 1% on 31 July, and on 3 August a joint US-Japan move pushed the dollar to a one-month low. Toyota's quarterly profit nearly doubled to $9.4 billion on the cheap yen that intervention is meant to reverse.

fx-rub.standing: The exchange rate of Russia's currency against the dollar, and the cleanest daily read on how sanctions, oil revenue and war spending are landing on the Russian economy. A weaker ruble raises the cost of every import and every foreign obligation.
fx-rub.recent: The ruble slid through a month of strikes reaching ever deeper into Russia: a drone attack on Nizhnekamsk, 1,600 km from the Ukrainian border, killed 13 and hit the Taneco refinery complex that funds much of the war, and drone strikes have kept hitting Wildberries' Russian warehouses. Moscow's Galuzin ruled out a freeze on 9 August.

fx-zar.standing: The exchange rate between South Africa's rand and the US dollar. The rand is one of the most heavily traded emerging-market currencies and a common proxy for risk appetite toward Africa, so it swings on commodity prices and global capital flows as much as on domestic news.
fx-zar.recent: The rand has firmed through the window, reaching its strongest level of the period on Aug 8 at 16.15 after a Jul 25 low point of 16.83. The domestic news in this period ran to governance and cost-of-living: electricity bills rose up to 14% this month after municipal surcharges, and a Prasa security-contract investigation drew fresh scrutiny in Pretoria. Neither explains the currency's path.

btc.standing: The price of one bitcoin, the first and largest cryptocurrency, quoted around the clock on exchanges worldwide. It has no issuer and no cashflow, so it trades on flows and on what holders believe it is for.
btc.recent: Bitcoin is roughly flat over the month, near $64,060 after peaking at $66,520 on Jul 22. Two custody failures set the tone: a Coldcard hack drained $120 million, with the attacker's own transactions congesting Bitcoin, and a separate exploit emptied Foundation's and Citadel21's Lightning nodes. ETFs still took in $754 million as volatility collapsed.

eth.standing: The second-largest cryptocurrency by value, and the settlement layer most stablecoins, tokens and exchange withdrawals actually run on. Its price reflects demand for that block space as much as speculation on the coin itself.
eth.recent: The month's swing sat inside a broad crypto retrenchment: over 100 crypto projects folded in 2026 alone, the Senate's Clarity Act missed its pre-recess vote window, and Treasury sanctioned an Iranian dollar-token exchange rather than a bank. On 9 August more than $8m was drawn out of Coinsbuy across TRON and Ethereum, and the exchange refilled the emptied wallets within 24 hours.

paxg.standing: A gold-backed token whose price tracks one troy ounce of physical gold, giving crypto markets a direct line to the metal investors buy when they doubt currencies, central banks or the safety of everything else.
paxg.recent: Gold rose about 8% over the past month, from $3,982 on Jul 17 to $4,406 on Aug 11, its high for the series. Binance began offering gold and silver options on 29 July after commodity futures drew billions in daily volume, and Tether's excess reserves — partly held in gold — halved to $4.11 billion from $8.23 billion.

wiki-artificial-intelligence.standing: A Wikipedia article whose daily readership rises when machine-learning systems make news. The pageview count is a rough gauge of how many people are trying to understand the technology at any given moment, rather than a measure of the field itself.
wiki-artificial-intelligence.recent: Stanford researchers used a model to design 16 working virus genomes — viruses not found in nature — and the story ran everywhere on 6 and 7 August. Zuckerberg's 6,500-word manifesto on superintelligence followed, alongside Nvidia arranging $500 billion in chip financing through six lenders and Meta releasing its Glimmer model to run on a single consumer GPU.

wiki-russia.standing: A count of how many people open the English Wikipedia article on Russia each day. It is a proxy for public curiosity rather than events, and it rises when a country moves from background to foreground in the news.
wiki-russia.recent: The peak on Aug 8 fell between two rounds of long-range strikes: drones forced nets over ballistic-missile submarines at Vilyuchinsk in Kamchatka, and on Aug 10 a drone attack killed 13 at Nizhnekamsk, 1,600 km from the Ukrainian border. Moscow separately ruled out a freeze in Ukraine.

wiki-pakistan.standing: Wikipedia's daily readership for the article on Pakistan, a nuclear-armed state of some 240 million people whose politics, security and economy draw attention far beyond South Asia. Readership rises when the country enters a wider story.
wiki-pakistan.recent: Readership climbed as Pakistan joined Saudi Arabia and Turkey in signing a joint defence pact in Mecca on 7 August — a collective-defence agreement that never states whose nuclear deterrent applies, and which Egypt declined to sign. Two suicide attacks preceded it, killing 14 at a peace rally in Swat on 2 August.

wiki-china.standing: The daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on China, a rough gauge of how many people worldwide are looking the country up. It rises when China is the subject of a story rather than the setting of one.
wiki-china.recent: The rise to the 10 August peak tracks Typhoon Dolphin: China closed major ports a day before landfall and evacuated over a million people, with flight cancellations across the coast as the storm came ashore at Yuhuan. The same week Beijing sanctioned six US entities and tightened drone exports, and codified Xinjiang's campaign-era restrictions into national law.

wiki-strait-of-hormuz.standing: The sea lane between Iran and Oman that connects the Gulf to the Indian Ocean, and the narrowest point in the world's oil trade. Roughly a fifth of global crude and much of its liquefied gas must pass through it, so the lane prices the region's risk.
wiki-strait-of-hormuz.recent: Iran has kept the strait closed, setting six conditions for reopening and adding a reparations clause that narrows the 60-day deal window to a week; Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi calls the US exchanges messages, not negotiations. Transits fell by a third, to 8 to 15 ships a day, with a tanker reporting two explosions near Kumzar.

wiki-bitcoin.standing: The number of people reading Wikipedia's Bitcoin article each day — a rough gauge of how far the asset has travelled beyond the people who already hold it, and one that tends to move when a price, a theft or a rule change reaches a general audience.
wiki-bitcoin.recent: Readership tracked a run of security failures rather than price: a Coldcard firmware bug drained $120 million, with the attacker's own transactions congesting Bitcoin, and a hardware wallet maker in Toronto destroyed inventory after thieves stole $88 million through one firmware bug. Attackers then drained Foundation's and Citadel21's Lightning nodes.

wiki-saudi-arabia.standing: The Wikipedia country article for Saudi Arabia, the Gulf's largest oil exporter and custodian of Islam's two holiest cities. Readership of a country page tends to move with the events that put it in front of people who do not normally follow it.
wiki-saudi-arabia.recent: The peak on 23 July fell in the run-up to Saudi Arabia joining US strikes on Iraq, its entry into the US-Iran war. Attention held through the Mecca defence pact signed 7 August by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan — read by some as a 'Sunni NATO' — and a Houthi strike on Najran that wounded 11, including a 4-year-old.

wiki-donald-trump.standing: The daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on the sitting US president. It rises when he acts rather than when he speaks, so its peaks mark the days a decision landed — a strike, a tariff, a firing.
wiki-donald-trump.recent: The series has fallen 18% over the month, and the traffic tracks the Iran file: Trump halted attacks on Iran's infrastructure on 2 August, then claimed the next day that the US fully controls the Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran describes differently. The lull since came as Hormuz talks with Iran and Oman made progress.

wiki-india.standing: The Wikipedia article on India, the world's most populous country and its largest democracy. Daily readership rises and falls with what the country is doing — elections, budgets, launches, disputes — and works as a rough gauge of global attention.
wiki-india.recent: The month's peak came before a run of stories now defining India's regulatory reach: Parliament enabled fees on the Unified Payments Interface, the CCPA fined dark patterns including Zepto's basket sneaking, and officials geoblocked Bitchat's GitHub code while leaving the mesh app untouched. Attention has since drifted lower.

wiki-israel.standing: How many people read the English Wikipedia article on Israel each day — a rough gauge of where public curiosity turns when the country is in the news, and one of the most-read country pages on the site.
wiki-israel.recent: Readership tracked the war's spread past Gaza: the July peak came as attention turned to Lebanon, where a seventh round of direct Beirut–Israel talks opened in Rome on 4 August and strikes continued through them, killing three around Tibnin and one at a cemetery prayer area. In Gaza, Netanyahu rejected the withdrawal sequencing and 1,257 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire.

wiki-united-states.standing: The daily count of people reading the English Wikipedia article on the United States. Baseline traffic is high and steady, so the swings are the interesting part: they mark the days a global audience went looking for context on Washington.
wiki-united-states.recent: The window is dominated by the US–Iran war and the Strait of Hormuz. Trump halted planned attacks on Iran's infrastructure on 2 August, then claimed on 3 August that the US fully controls the strait; by 4–5 August, talks with Iran and Oman to reopen it were reported as making progress. Saudi strikes in Iraq on 29 July marked Riyadh's entry into the war.

wiki-ukraine.standing: Daily readership of Wikipedia's Ukraine article, a rough gauge of how many people are looking the country up rather than reading about it. It climbs when the war forces its way onto front pages abroad and drifts down when attention moves elsewhere.
wiki-ukraine.recent: The month-long slide broke with the drone strike on Nizhnekamsk, 1,600 km from the Ukrainian border, which killed 13 including a child. Days before, Galuzin ruled out a freeze on Moscow's behalf, and a strike on Dnipro burned 170 of 300 pallets of WHO medical aid.

wiki-nigeria.standing: Daily readership of the English Wikipedia article on Nigeria, Africa's most populous country and its largest economy. Attention here rises when the country's politics, security or economy break into global news.
wiki-nigeria.recent: Readership fell back through early August after a late-July peak, with the news since spread across separate fronts rather than one story: US strikes in West Africa, a Sahel bloc summons of Nigeria's top diplomat over security attribution, and an alleged coup-funding trail in which a currency dealer moved 785 million naira to plotters. Domestically, Tinubu ordered the EFCC to vacate the Osun account freeze order.

cp:hormuz.standing: One-fifth of global seaborne oil passes through this 21-mile strait between Iran and Oman.
cp:hormuz.recent: Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz closed, setting six conditions through Omani mediation and adding a reparations clause that narrowed the 60-day deal window to a week; 8 to 15 ships now cross daily against a normal flow many times that. Iraqi crude has begun moving overland through Syria, and Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia has dropped.

cp:bab-el-mandeb.standing: Between Yemen and Djibouti — the Red Sea’s southern gate. Houthi attacks since 2023 have pushed container shipping to reroute around Africa.
cp:bab-el-mandeb.recent: Traffic fell as the Houthis widened their war: missiles and drones hit the Red Sea port of Mokha, a projectile sank the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya, and escort requests for Saudi tankers jumped 39% since February. Crossings dropped to 18 ships on a Sunday from 28 the Friday before.

cp:suez.standing: Egypt’s 120-mile artery carries roughly 12% of global trade. The 2021 closure disrupted supply chains for weeks; Red Sea instability keeps it volatile.
cp:suez.recent: Attacks on the southern approach set the traffic. A projectile strike sank the Indian-flagged MSV Faize Noore Oliya off Mokha on 4 August, and 18 ships crossed Bab El-Mandeb on Sunday against 28 on Friday. Vessels that avoid the strait never reach Suez, holding transits near the 90-day baseline rather than the 50 counted on Jun 25.

cp:malacca.standing: Between Malaysia and Sumatra — the fastest route between the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Over 80,000 ships a year, including most of China’s oil imports.
cp:malacca.recent: Traffic recovered to 246 vessels a day, well above the 170 low on Jul 19 and roughly back to the Jun 22 high, running 1.7% above the 90-day baseline with no weather alert. The Hormuz closure sits behind part of the mix: Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia has dropped, and Hormuz vessel transits have fallen to a fraction, pushing Asian refiners toward cargoes that reach them by other routes.

cp:taiwan.standing: Between mainland China and Taiwan — roughly 40% of the world’s container traffic passes through, and the flashpoint of any US–China confrontation.
cp:taiwan.recent: Traffic swung hard around Typhoon Dolphin: China closed major ports a full day before the expected landfall, evacuating over a million people, and vessel counts collapsed to 28 on Jul 10 before rebounding to a 401 peak on Jul 12 as backlogged ships cleared. The last week sits level with the 90-day baseline.

cp:panama.standing: 50-mile shortcut between the Atlantic and Pacific. Drought in 2023–24 cut daily transits by half — a live example of climate binding to trade.
cp:panama.recent: Traffic has thinned by about a fifth across the window, from 83 vessels a day on Jul 13 to 27 now, with the floor at 22 on Jul 22 — though the last week sits close to the 90-day baseline. The input does not name a cause at the canal itself. It arrives in a summer of record heat and low water elsewhere: sea surface hit 20.96°C in July, France's Seine is running dangerously low, and drought pushed Danube reactors toward shutdown.

cp:bosporus.standing: Istanbul’s 20-mile waterway links the Black Sea to the Mediterranean — the only route for Russian naval access and Ukrainian grain exports.
cp:bosporus.recent: Traffic has thinned as a drone campaign made the Black Sea run uninsurable: drones struck the Turkish-operated Nadezhda near Novorossiysk on 4 August, sank a Rosatom freighter off the same port, and killed a crewman on a coal-hauling tanker. Turkey has since turned back some vessels bound for Novorossiysk.

cp:gibraltar.standing: 8 miles between Morocco and Spain — the only Atlantic–Mediterranean link. A surveillance chokepoint for Russian submarines and sanctioned oil.
cp:gibraltar.recent: Traffic through the strait is running about 3% below its 90-day baseline, at 125 vessels a day. Over the window it swung between 111 on Jun 3 and 163 on Jun 13, with calm seas throughout — maximum waves of 0.6 m. Nothing in the record explains the swing.

cp:dover.standing: The busiest shipping lane on Earth — 400+ ships a day squeeze through the English Channel’s 21-mile narrows.
cp:dover.recent: Traffic sits close to its own 90-day baseline, with calm water — waves under a metre — and no weather alert. The 82-day swing from 210 vessels a day on May 23 to 130 on Jun 29 is the ordinary range for this lane; nothing in the window explains it as a disruption.

cp:cape-of-good-hope.standing: The 3,000-mile detour around southern Africa — the alternative when the Red Sea is closed. The new default for tankers since Houthi attacks began.
cp:cape-of-good-hope.recent: Traffic has eased to 97 vessels a day, well below the 161 counted on May 15 and 8.7% under its own 90-day baseline over the past week. Rough seas ran with it, waves reaching 3.4 metres at the latest reading.

cp:kerch.standing: Between Crimea and Russia — the only access to the Sea of Azov. A flashpoint since 2014 and contested throughout the Russia–Ukraine war.
cp:kerch.recent: Traffic has fallen to zero, roughly 90 percent below its own 90-day baseline, with the last vessels counted before mid-July. The waters sit inside a war that is now reaching far beyond the front: a drone strike killed 13 at Nizhnekamsk, 1,600 km from the Ukrainian border, and a drone killed one crewman on a coal-hauling tanker.

mkt:tadawul.standing: The Arab world’s largest exchange by market value, dominated by Aramco. Trades Sunday to Thursday, so it opens the global week before Tokyo.
mkt:tadawul.recent: Saudi Arabia has been drawn into the region's war on both ends: it joined US strikes in Iraq in late July, and Houthi missiles have since hit Najran, Marib and the Jazan refinery that processes 400,000 barrels of crude daily. The index has drifted down through that, even as war-driven oil lifted Aramco profit 33%.

mkt:bist.standing: Türkiye’s only exchange. Priced in lira, so its index level carries the country’s inflation as much as its earnings — read the direction, not the number.
mkt:bist.recent: Parliament passed the law dissolving and disarming the PKK late Monday, closing a 40-year insurgency; the index rose 0.23% on the day. The rest of the two-month decline runs alongside war-risk pressure on Turkish shipping — a drone strike on the cargo ship Nadezhda near Novorossiysk, and Ankara rationing Bosphorus passage.

mkt:dfm.standing: The Gulf’s main listing venue for property and banking. Moved from a Sunday–Thursday week to Monday–Friday in 2022, unlike Riyadh.
mkt:dfm.recent: The index sits below its Jun 18 high of 6270 after a run of Dubai-specific shocks: seven blasts in twenty minutes hit Jebel Ali port on 5 August, the emirate's transshipment core, and Iran pressed demands for an Iranian-controlled inbound lane through Hormuz, the strait Dubai's cargo depends on. The extradition of Kinahan the same week closed a decade of exile in Dubai.

mkt:bursa-malaysia.standing: The world’s largest market for Islamic finance instruments, and the centre of the global sukuk trade.
mkt:bursa-malaysia.recent: The index has drifted lower as the Hormuz closure worked its way into Malaysian refineries: Gulf crude arriving in Malaysia has dropped, with vessel transits through the strait falling to a fraction of normal. Politics compounded it — Anwar Ibrahim's coalition lost Negeri Sembilan to a Malay-nationalist wave on 3 August, and the DAP scheduled a vote on staying in the unity government.

mkt:idx.standing: The exchange of the world’s largest Muslim-majority country, heavily weighted to commodities and banking.
mkt:idx.recent: The index has given up 8.6% over the past three months, well below its May 11 peak of 6,906. Nothing in the Jakarta news flow explains the slide: the period's stories run to a ferry fire off Madura, a drug case against a Malaysian pilot, and deepening losses at the state-backed Whoosh high-speed rail line — none of them market-moving on this scale.

mkt:tse.standing: Asia’s largest exchange, and the first major market to price each trading day.
mkt:tse.recent: A cheap yen has been doing the work: Toyota's quarterly profit nearly doubled to $9.4 billion on the weak currency and solid demand, and the Bank of Japan held rates at 1%. The counterweight arrived on 3 August, when a joint US-Japan intervention pushed the dollar to a one-month low.

mkt:hkex.standing: Where mainland Chinese companies meet foreign capital — the clearest daily read on sentiment toward China.
mkt:hkex.recent: The index sits near the bottom of a 64-day range that peaked at 26,410 on May 11 and bottomed at 22,670 on Jun 26, and fell 0.6% on the day. Typhoon Dolphin forced China to close major ports a day before landfall and evacuate over a million people, and Mercedes cut its sales outlook on weak China demand.

mkt:sse.standing: Mainland China’s main board. Largely closed to foreign investors, so it tracks domestic policy more than global risk appetite.
mkt:sse.recent: The index has drifted down about 6% over the window, from its May 13 high to a July 17 low near 3,764. Industrial demand news has run against it: Mercedes cut its sales outlook on weak China, Tesla was reported weighing a sale of its China business, and Typhoon Dolphin forced port closures and the evacuation of over a million people before landfall.

mkt:krx.standing: Dominated by Samsung and SK Hynix — a proxy for the global semiconductor cycle.
mkt:krx.recent: The index is a memory trade. Samsung profit surged 1,814% on AI chip demand and Samsung warned of shortage through 2028, driving a record 18% single-day gain on 31 July that reclaimed the 6,500-point level after the steepest three-day rout preceding it. SK Hynix then dropped 5% on approving $38B in new memory fabs.

mkt:bse.standing: Asia’s oldest exchange, founded 1875, and the benchmark for Indian equities.

mkt:sgx.standing: Southeast Asia’s financial hub, weighted to banks and regional property.
mkt:sgx.recent: The index reached 5745 on Aug 11, its highest in the 64-day series and roughly 16 percent above the May 11 low of 4943. The available reporting does not explain the advance.

mkt:twse.standing: TSMC alone is roughly a third of the index, which makes this the most concentrated major market on the map.
mkt:twse.recent: The index has recovered from its 30 July low, though the ground under it is uneven: chipmaking employs few of Taiwan's workers, leaving a two-speed economy where the boom is concentrated in fabs. Two Chinese coast guard ships drifted off Orchid Island, east of Taiwan, on 31 July, near the series trough.

mkt:set.standing: Thailand’s benchmark, sensitive to tourism flows and regional energy prices.
mkt:set.recent: The index has recovered from its May low but slipped on the day, with Bangkok absorbing two political shocks in one week: the visit of Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing, who led the 2021 coup, and a school shooting in Nonthaburi that killed eight and wounded 15, after which the Thai PM vowed stricter gun laws.

mkt:pse.standing: A small, domestically-driven market where remittance flows move the index.
mkt:pse.recent: The index sits near the top of its 49-day range after climbing from its late-May low, with a drop on the latest session. The available reporting from Manila covers South China Sea friction and a magnitude 6.3 earthquake in the southern Philippines on 5 August, neither of which explains the market's path.

mkt:asx.standing: Mining and banking. Often the first major market to react to Chinese demand data.
mkt:asx.recent: The index reached 9,272 on Aug 6, the top of a 66-day run of roughly 4%, days after China's steel stock aged into recycling territory — a shift toward scrap that skips Australian iron ore, the export the index leans on hardest. Critical minerals have not filled the gap: Australia's new mines lack separation capacity.

mkt:jse.standing: Africa’s largest exchange by far, and the continent’s only one with a usable public daily series.
mkt:jse.recent: The index sits below where it started the window, with the low on Jul 23 and a partial recovery since. Domestic cost pressure is one backdrop: electricity bills rose up to 14% this month after municipal surcharge increases in Johannesburg. Nothing in the available material explains the day-to-day moves further.

mkt:b3.standing: Latin America’s largest exchange, driven by iron ore, oil and Brazilian rates.
mkt:b3.recent: The index has drifted about 5% below its May high through a run of friction with Washington. Brazil requested WTO consultations over US tariffs on 28 July, filing a trade case it can't finish, and on 4 August the US revoked the visa of Brazil's ambassador, saying it will restore it if Brasília accepts its envoy pick. Lula was nominated for a fourth term on 2 August.

mkt:bmv.standing: Mexico’s benchmark, tightly coupled to US demand and the peso.
mkt:bmv.recent: The index sits below where it started the window despite the day's rise, and the input does not identify what drove the move.

mkt:byma.standing: Priced in a currency that has lost most of its value repeatedly, so the index rises even in bad years. Direction over a day means something; the level does not.

mkt:tsx.standing: Energy, mining and banks — a commodity index wearing an equity index’s clothes.

mkt:nyse.standing: The largest equity market on earth. Its close sets the tone every other market opens against.
mkt:nyse.recent: The index sits near its high for the window after a run that has taken it up roughly 5% since June. The Washington news flow around it has been mostly regulatory and geopolitical rather than corporate: the Senate advanced the crypto Clarity Act, a bill taxing buyers of Russian oil, Treasury sanctions on Iranian dollar-token exchanges, and Trump's renewed attempt to remove Fed governor Cook.

mkt:lse.standing: Most FTSE 100 revenue is earned abroad, so a falling pound tends to push the index up.
mkt:lse.recent: The index sits near the high it set on 29 July, up around 6% across the window. The London coverage in this period is domestic and regulatory rather than market-moving — a ban on inflated "was" prices for retailers, and a bill folding Healthwatch England into the National Health Service — and none of it explains the move.

mkt:xetra.standing: Germany’s industrial and chemical base — Europe’s clearest export barometer.
mkt:xetra.recent: The index reached 26,320 on Aug 10, the top of a 66-day run of roughly 8%, despite the carmakers cutting: BMW is cutting 8,000 jobs worldwide, Porsche another 5,000, and Mercedes cut its sales outlook on weak China. The strength came from elsewhere — Adidas reported strong growth thanks to the World Cup, and Commerzbank said teaming up with UniCredit could create value.

mkt:euronext-paris.standing: Luxury goods and energy dominate — unusually exposed to Chinese consumer demand.
mkt:euronext-paris.recent: The index has climbed steadily from its 7,953 low on May 15 to a fresh high of 8,726 on Aug 10, a gain of about 8% across the period. No single event in the available reporting accounts for the rise.

mkt:euronext-amsterdam.standing: The world’s oldest exchange, now carried largely by ASML.
mkt:euronext-amsterdam.recent: The index closed at its 66-day high on Aug 10, roughly a tenth above the May 12 low, with Shell agreeing on Aug 3 to sell its European onshore renewables business.

mkt:bme.standing: Spanish banks with heavy Latin American exposure make this a proxy for both regions.
mkt:bme.recent: The index rose about 13% over the window to a high of 20,180 on Aug 6, then slipped to 20,170. Spanish news through the period ran to the Ceuta crossings, where 72,000 people entered a city of 84,000 and Italy suspended Schengen against Spain, but nothing in that coverage explains the equity move.

mkt:borsa-italiana.standing: Banks and utilities, and the market most sensitive to Italian sovereign debt spreads.
mkt:borsa-italiana.recent: The index closed at its 67-day high on 7 August, up about 9 percent over the window, as Italy's border dispute with Spain escalated without touching trade. Rome had suspended Schengen against Spain on 31 July after 72,000 people rushed the Ceuta enclave, and Madrid imposed reciprocal checks on 7 August. Milan-based Bending Spoons bought Airtable for $1.28bn on 4 August.

mkt:six.standing: Nestlé, Roche and Novartis carry the index, which makes it defensive when the world turns risk-off.
mkt:six.recent: The index closed at 14,630 on 10 August, its high for the 64-day window and up 11.7% from the 13,100 low on 11 May. Nothing in the available material explains the climb.

mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.standing: Nordic industrials and telecoms, and a useful early read on European capital spending.
mkt:nasdaq-stockholm.recent: The index sits near the top of its 65-day range after climbing from a 15 May low of 3036 to a 5 August high of 3327, easing 0.3% on the day. The coverage in this window points at Volkswagen, where the controlling families broke board silence to press management over excess capacity — a signal to the European industrial complex Stockholm's exporters sit inside.

mkt:tase.standing: Trades Sunday to Thursday. Heavily weighted to banks, defence and technology.
mkt:tase.recent: The index has fallen about 9.5% over the past three months, from a high of 4,463 on May 11 to 4,039, with a low of 3,966 on Jun 29. The available material does not explain the decline.

poly-israel-x-iran-ceasefire-continues-t.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the ceasefire between Israel and Iran holds through the market's deadline. It trades as a percentage, so the price is what buyers will pay for that outcome, and it moves whenever the terms of the truce are tested.
poly-israel-x-iran-ceasefire-continues-t.recent: The price climbed from 34 on Jul 19 to 97 on Aug 11 as the confrontation moved from strikes to procedure. Trump cancelled attacks on Iran's infrastructure on Aug 2, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi put an Oman-brokered agreement on new Hormuz shipping lanes in its final stages. Iran's damaged airports reopened, though the strait stays closed pending a US act.

poly-will-united-russia-er-gain-the-most.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether United Russia, the governing party, wins the most seats in Russia's next State Duma election. The price is what traders will pay for that outcome, so it moves with anything that changes the party's grip on the vote.
poly-will-united-russia-er-gain-the-most.recent: The contract rose through a month in which the war reached deep into Russia itself: Ukraine struck two refineries on 6 August, including Yaroslavl, and a drone attack on Nizhnekamsk killed 13 people 1,600 km from the Ukrainian border. Moscow hardened rather than bent — Deputy Foreign Minister Galuzin ruled out a freeze on 9 August.

xag.standing: A silver-backed token priced against an ounce of silver. Silver is both a precious metal held as a store of value and an industrial input — solar cells, electronics, brazing — so it moves on money and on manufacturing at once.
xag.recent: Silver ended the window at 63.32 an ounce on Aug 11, its 31-day high and 8.91% above where the series began. The single 29.8 print on Aug 6 sits far below every reading around it. Nothing here explains the move.

wiki-spain.standing: The daily count of people opening the English Wikipedia article on Spain. Attention series like it spike when a country enters a story large enough that readers go looking for the basics behind it.
wiki-spain.recent: Views peaked at 117,100 on Jul 20 during the Ceuta crossings, when nearly 60,000 people swam around the enclave's border fence in a week and 57 bodies were recovered; Italy then suspended Schengen and reimposed border checks against Spain, and Spain reciprocated. Traffic has since fallen back to 9,772.

poly-will-the-fed-increase-interest-rate.standing: A Polymarket contract on whether the US Federal Reserve raises its policy rate by 25 basis points at the coming decision. The price is what traders pay for that outcome, so it moves with anything that shifts the odds of a hike rather than a hold or a cut.
poly-will-the-fed-increase-interest-rate.recent: The Fed held rates at 350-375 basis points on 29 July, citing 'elevated' inflation, and signalled rates could still rise — a hold that analysts read as hawkish, and Citadel had bet on a hike outright. The contract peaked at 60% on 1 August; it has since drifted back to 41% as Trump moved again to fire Cook, reviving the fight over Fed independence.

poly-total-internet-blackout-in-iran-by-.standing: A Polymarket contract paying out if Iran's internet is fully cut off nationwide before a set date. Its price is what traders will pay for that outcome, and it tracks how close observers think Tehran is to sealing the country off during a crisis.
poly-total-internet-blackout-in-iran-by-.recent: The contract has fallen from 42% on Jul 21 to 9% as the Hormuz standoff moved toward a deal rather than an escalation: Trump halted attacks on Iran's infrastructures on 2 August, Oman-brokered talks on reopening the strait made progress, and Iran reopened its damaged airports. Araghchi says messages, not negotiations.

stocks:PLTR.standing: A US software company that builds data-integration and analytics platforms, sold mainly to defence, intelligence and immigration agencies alongside large corporates. Its revenue depends heavily on government contracting.
stocks:PLTR.recent: The stock has run from $122.30 on Jul 30 to $175.20 on Aug 10. The move began with a 30% surge on Aug 4 that cost short sellers $3bn in a single day, and continued as federal buying of commercial data stayed in view — ICE agreeing to pay LexisNexis $6.7 million for data.
